analysis.one_liner: Sends monthly child tax credit payments to families and sharply expands the earned income credit for low-wage workers.
analysis.headline: S. 1992 was introduced in June 2023 with 43 cosponsors — all Democrats or independents — and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a markup or a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the child tax credit fully refundable and pay it out monthly — $250 per child per month, $300 for children under 6 — so even families that owe no income tax would receive the full amount. It would also permanently enlarge the earned income tax credit for workers without children: lowering the eligibility age from 25 to 19, removing the age-65 cutoff, and roughly doubling the phase-in rate so childless low-wage workers could receive a much larger credit. The bill contained no revenue offsets, meaning the expanded credits would add to federal deficits.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children, who would receive monthly cash payments even if they owe little or no income tax, and low-wage workers without children, a group the current earned income credit largely shuts out.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the child tax credit fully refundable, so families with little or no income tax liability receive the full credit rather than a partial one.
It provides monthly advance payments of $250 per child ($300 for children under 6), putting cash in families' hands during the year instead of as a once-a-year tax refund.

It permanently expands the earned income credit for workers without children: eligibility age drops from 25 to 19, the age-65 cap is eliminated, and the phase-in rate doubles from 7.65% to 15.3%, substantially raising the maximum credit for childless low-wage workers.
It lets workers use the prior year's earnings to calculate the earned income credit, smoothing the credit for people whose income drops in a given year.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, since the bill text contains no revenue offsets and the expanded credits would be deficit-financed; higher-income households are largely phased out of the expanded credits.

drawbacks.text: The bill text contains no revenue provisions to pay for the expanded credits, so the cost would be added to federal deficits.

Monthly advance payments can leave families owing money back at tax time if their income or family circumstances change mid-year; the bill devotes extensive provisions to recapturing overpayments, which highlights the risk.

Making the child credit fully refundable removes the earnings-based floor in current law, so a family with no earnings would receive the full credit — a design choice critics say weakens any connection between the credit and work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and well-targeted: tens of millions of working families would get direct monthly cash, and the childless-worker credit fixes a long-recognized gap that excludes young and older low-wage workers. The cost is real and unaddressed — the bill simply omits any pay-fors, leaving the financing to future Congresses — and the monthly-payment design carries overpayment risks that would fall on the same families it aims to help.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the Working Families Tax Relief Act of 2023 on June 14, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
Forty-three senators cosponsored the bill — 41 Democrats and 2 independents — but no Republican signed on.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained anything new; the outcome preserved the status quo, in which working families keep the smaller permanent credits and the Treasury keeps the revenue a larger, unoffset credit expansion would have paid out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody; families keep smaller credits, Treasury keeps revenue

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 43 cosponsors.

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the first cosponsor of the expanded child tax credit design.

for.name: 41 Democrats and 2 independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it unanimous Democratic-side support in the Senate.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but his committee never scheduled a markup or vote, leaving the bill to die without action.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill; with no Republican support and the Senate's 60-vote threshold for most legislation, the bill had no path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 43 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; not one Republican senator signed on [S4], and the bill's fate was sealed in a committee whose chair was himself a cosponsor [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill's credit phase-outs begin at $150,000 for joint filers and $112,500 for others, with a second phase-out above those levels, so higher earners receive little or nothing from the expanded credits [S3]. The exclusion is a deliberate targeting choice rather than a new tax.
The bill text contains no revenue offsets, so the expanded credits would be deficit-financed, adding to costs borne by all federal taxpayers [S3].
